segments.say: Yesterday this folder was empty. Today it has a simulator, tests, a plugin and a set of rules, and none of it was typed by me. The three files in that tree are still marked U — untracked. Nothing here has ever been committed. Hold that thought; it comes back at the end as the thing we got wrong. So today is the awkward day. Not how do I get an agent to build something — how do I keep it useful once the thing it is working in has grown. And we are going to be honest about our own project rather than talk in general terms. Because this is where most people quietly lose. The first day with an agent feels like magic. The tenth day, on a codebase with history, is where it either keeps working or turns into something you fight.

You do not get an error. You get answers that are slightly less grounded than last week's, and you carry on, because they still sound right. I am asking it to walk seven habits that keep an agent effective in a large codebase, and for each one to point at a real file here, or say plainly that we do not have it. Watch how the answers land, because roughly half of them are gaps. It finds documentation at every level and a memory file that tells it where the truth lives. It finds a rule that fires by itself — and reads back the comment where that rule documents its own limits. Emoji detection is exact, because that is a property of the character. Name detection is a heuristic, and the file says so: it cannot tell that Morgan is a person while Preston is a town. And then the sentence I would frame. A pass means nothing obvious. It never means no personal data. The rule still lives with whoever writes the code. That is what accountability actually looks like once you have automated something. The check does not absolve you. It narrows what you have to look at. It also finds real gaps. No code owners file. No pull request template. And no review has ever happened here at all. Read the shape of that answer, not just the content. I asked seven questions and got four yeses and three gaps, with a file path against every claim. An agent that tells you what is missing in your own project is doing something much more useful than one that tells you it looks great. And the reason it can do that at all is everything we built yesterday. It is not guessing at good practice in the abstract — it is reading our brief, our memory file, our hook, and comparing them against what is actually on disk. There is one more thing worth pulling out of that answer before we move on, because it is the habit underneath all seven. Every single claim it made came with a path. Not it looks like you have documentation - here is the file, here is the line. When you are working in a codebase you did not write line by line, the citation is the product. An assertion without one is a guess wearing a suit. And it is worth being clear about why an agent can audit a project like this at all, because it is not insight. It is that everything it is checking against is written down in the repository: the brief, the memory file, the hook, the plan. If those files did not exist, the same seven questions would produce seven paragraphs of generic advice. The audit is only as good as the standard you wrote before you asked for it.

Then I ask it to fix something in our own memory file — to find anything we drag into every session but only occasionally need, and convert it to a link. And it declines. There is no at-tag left to convert, because we already did this on day one. But read what it does instead of stopping, because it puts a number on the decision. The brief is five and a half thousand bytes, about fourteen hundred tokens, and importing it would be paid on every session whether or not that session ever opens a requirement. The memory file itself is three hundred and sixty. So inlining the plan would make the always-on cost roughly five times larger, for content most sessions never read. And it points out where at-tags do belong: inside the two commands, which only load when you invoke them, and which exist specifically to compare the code against the brief. That is the rule in one line. Always-needed gets inlined. Occasionally-needed gets a path. And notice it went further than the question. While re-reading the file it spotted that we tell people to run a start script that does not exist yet, and flagged it without fixing it. That is the right instinct: a documentation bug is still a bug, and it is not the thing I asked about. And that number is the part to copy. Not the specific decision - our memory file is small and yours will be different.

The method: work out what a thing costs on every session, work out how often it is actually read, and let those two numbers decide. Most arguments about what belongs in a memory file evaporate the moment somebody counts. Now the part of this lecture I actually care about. I asked it to write the kind of test suite a coverage target produces. Aim for eighty percent, mock whatever gets in the way. And it does, cheerfully: twenty tests, ninety-one percent coverage, comfortably past target, all green. And the ninety-one is not a made-up number. It measured coverage with the standard library's own tracer, no extra dependency, and it noticed that Python here is three point nine and picked the older instruction-line API accordingly. The measurement is honest. It is the thing being measured that is worthless. Then it does the thing nobody does. It runs those same twenty tests against a deliberately broken simulator. A tick that moves nothing. A hold that holds nothing. An exception feed with no limit. Three real outages. All twenty still pass. Sit with that. The suite cannot tell a working simulator from a broken one. And then it breaks down how. Five tests are shape and type checks that go green against an empty fleet. Two named for determinism compare a string to the string they just passed in. Three assert only that nothing raised — including one that catches an exception a mock was configured to throw. Three never load the simulator at all; they assert that a mock records calls. Three are tautologies — the estimate test recomputes the expected value with the same expression as the code, so both sides move together on any change, including a wrong one. That accounts for sixteen. The last four are the ones with a real requirement behind them and an assertion that does not quite reach it — and those four are the ones that survive the next step. Keep them in mind. And the single best detail in the whole day. There is a test called the-exception-feed-is-capped-at-fifty. It injects three exceptions and asserts that three is not more than fifty. The line that actually enforces the cap is one of the four lines the suite never executes. Named for the requirement. Green forever. Never touches the code that implements it. And it prints the line, so there is nothing to take on faith: line seventy-seven, the slice that keeps the last fifty exceptions and throws the rest away. Four lines in the whole module never ran, and that is one of them. The requirement had a test, the test had the right name, and the code that satisfies the requirement was never executed once. That is not an unusual failure. It is the ordinary consequence of naming a test after a requirement instead of writing one that exercises it. And be clear about who wrote those tests. I did. I asked for exactly this, in those words — aim for eighty percent, mock whatever gets in the way — and I got precisely what I asked for. That is the trap. And notice which part of the request did the damage. Not the eighty percent — the four words after it. Mock whatever gets in the way is an instruction to remove the system under test whenever the system under test is inconvenient. Say that sentence out loud to yourself before you ever type it. Nobody would agree to it in those terms, and it is what a coverage target quietly asks for every time. The agent is extremely good at hitting the target you name. So the target had better be the thing you actually want. One more thing about why this matters more with an agent than it did before. A person writing twenty bad tests takes a week, and gets bored, and starts asking whether this is worth it. An agent writes them in ninety seconds and never asks. Every quality problem you had before is now available at a hundred times the speed, which means the checks you used to be able to skip are the ones you now have to automate. And there is a specific reason mocking is where this goes wrong. A mock is a statement about how the code is currently written. Change the implementation and the mock is wrong; keep the implementation and the mock proves nothing you did not already know.

So we reject it. I ask which of those would survive a rewrite of the simulator, and which would break for no good reason — and to delete the ones that exist only to move the number. The first thing it does is tell me my question was wrong. Eighteen of the twenty survive a rewrite from scratch — and that is not a defence of them. They survive because they assert almost nothing. A test that survives every rewrite and every bug is not a durable test, it is an executed line. So it swaps in a better filter, and this is the sentence to steal: if this broke on a Tuesday, would this test be the thing that told me? Twenty become four. And look at the result, because it is the whole argument of this lecture in two lines. Against the working simulator, four passing. Against the broken one, three of the four fail. Four tests catch the three outages that twenty missed. Fewer tests. Lower coverage. And it fails on the thing it is named for. Ninety-one percent down to eighty, and the count of the three outages caught goes from zero to three. Put those two numbers together and coverage stops being a quality measure and becomes what it is: a measure of how much code you ran. And four of them were not deleted, they were rewritten, because they had a real requirement behind them and an assertion that missed it. The cap test is the clearest. It used to inject three exceptions and check that three was under fifty. Now it injects past fifty and measures the list the simulator actually keeps — because a read that slices to fifty looks capped over a list that grows all day. Notice something it did on its own initiative too: before overwriting, it copied the original file, because nothing here is committed to git and the work would have been unrecoverable. Nobody asked. Which is the last habit, and the one we have been failing all along. Work cut small enough to review. In the code, yes — eight files, none longer than two hundred and thirty lines, requirements numbered so a command can check one at a time. But the honest answer is no. Git has no commits. Seventeen hundred lines of source and tests, the plugin, all the configuration — one untracked pile. No branch, no commit, no diff that anybody could review. The habit is designed into the file layout and completely absent from the history. And that is exactly the shape of the mistake this whole lecture is about: it is very easy to have the appearance of discipline, and no record of it at all. So take two things out of this lecture. First: never ask for a coverage number. Ask for tests that fail when the behaviour is wrong, and check that by breaking the code on purpose and watching them go red. If they stay green, you have decoration, not tests. Second: commit early and commit in pieces. Not because git is virtuous, but because review is the only thing standing between you and a very large amount of plausible code — and you cannot review a pile. It closed with something I did not ask for and would not have found. The same blind spot exists in our real test suite — line one hundred of the exceptions test — and it checked the production code before saying so, which is correct there. The code caps the list properly. The test simply cannot prove it. That is the shape of the bug you should be most afraid of: right code, green test, no relationship between the two. And notice what the deletion actually bought. Not tidiness. A suite that can fail. That is the only property of a test suite that matters, and it is the one a coverage percentage cannot see. And do not take the number four as a target either. The point is not fewer tests. The point is that every test in the suite has a failure it is capable of catching, and you know what it is.
